text.p: Colombia denied on Monday that its military had entered into a U.S.-backed alliance with right-wing paramilitary groups waging a "dirty war" against suspected left-wing rebel sympathisers.

The charge is contained in a report by New York-based Human Rights Watch made available at a news conference in Bogota. The report accuses Washington of official complicity in the covert war and calls for an immediate cutoff of all U.S. military aid to Colombia.

Entitled "Colombia's Killer Networks," the report echoes charges made last month by Amnesty International about an alliance between the military and rightist gunmen -- or death squads -- who killed with impunity across Colombia for years.
Defence Minister Juan Carlos Esguerra, speaking with the Caracol radio network on Monday, denied such an alliance existed, saying, "I reject (the charge) categorically."

He conceded there might have been isolated cases in the past in which individual military officers had links to the paramilitary. But Esguerra, reported to be a possible candidate to fill Colombia's vacant ambassadorial post in Washington, said there was no "strategic institutional alliance" between the military and irregular armed groups.
Human rights groups said there is overwhelming evidence to the contrary and the United States has been a willing partner in covering the alliance up.

"This is a sophisticated mechanism, in part supported by years of advice, training, weaponry and official silence by the United States, that allows the Colombian military to fight a dirty war and Colombian officialdom to deny it," Jose Miguel Vivanco, executive director of Human Rights Watch/Americas, said in a statement prepared for release at the news conference on Monday.
"The price so far is thousands of dead, disappeared, maimed and terrorised Colombians," he added.

In its report, Human Rights Watch alleged a team assembled by the CIA and the U.S. Defence Department worked with the Colombian military on restructuring its intelligence-gathering capabilities in 1991 in an effort that led directly to the creation of paramilitary "killer networks."

Additionally, it said Washington has provided weapons, ostensibly to fight drugs, to Colombian military units with a record of serious human rights abuse without ensuring U.S. aid is not used to commit further abuse.
The report urged the immediate suspension of all U.S. military aid to Colombia -- a country immersed in a low-intensity war with leftist guerrillas since the mid-1960s.
